Training in Arms and the Duty to Protect

Dawn rises over the hills of Anórien. Since the previous day, a cold wind has been descending from the heights, driving long bands of cloud above the lands between Minas Tirith and the Anduin. In a small stone fortification beside the road to Cair Andros, the men of the garrison are completing their first change of watch. The sentries return to their quarters, while the soldiers assigned to the morning watch take their places upon the walls.

In the courtyard, a man in his forties inspects the equipment of twelve warriors assembled before him. He wears a carefully maintained coat of mail, a dark surcoat, and a sword hanging at his side. His shield rests against the nearby wall. An old scar crosses his left cheek, and his hair is beginning to grey at the temples.

He stops before a young soldier whose shield strap is too loose. Without raising his voice, he asks the man to lift his arm, checks the fastening, and shows him how to tighten it. Another carries a spear whose point bears traces of rust. The veteran sends him to fetch the tools needed to clean it before the patrol departs.

For more than twenty years he has served in the forces of Gondor. He began as an ordinary man-at-arms in a garrison of the southern provinces before taking part in several campaigns along the Anduin. He knows the weariness of prolonged marches, the weight of armour in the rain, and the long hours spent waiting for an enemy whose intentions remain unknown.

He knows the men under his command as well. Some have served beside him for years; others have only recently completed their training. Two have never yet taken part in a real battle.

A rider enters the courtyard just as the patrol is preparing to leave. His horse is flecked with foam, and his cloak bears the marks of a long ride. He brings troubling news: several Orcs were sighted during the night near an old passage leading down to the riverbanks. A second patrol, sent to reconnoitre the area, has not returned.

The veteran listens to the messenger, then asks to examine the map kept in the guardroom. The reported passage lies less than two hours' march away. A secondary track approaches it from the heights, but part of the force will have to pass through a narrow valley where the trees offer ample cover.

He divides the men into two groups. The best archers will accompany an experienced scout to the ridge, while the others advance under his command along the main path. He reminds them of their agreed signals, checks their weapons one final time, and gives the order to depart.

The soldiers leave the fortification shortly after sunrise.

As they approach the passage, they discover the first traces of the enemy. A branch has been broken at the height of a man; farther on, several footprints mark the damp earth. The veteran orders the patrol to slow down. The men close their ranks and ready their shields.

An arrow suddenly flies from the trees and strikes the rim of a shield. Other missiles follow almost at once. The soldiers draw closer together, protecting their companions while the archers try to identify the enemy positions.

The veteran glimpses several figures descending towards the path. He orders his men to hold the line and steps forward to reinforce the gap through which the attackers are trying to force their way. A heavy blow strikes his shield; he drives his opponent back, regains his balance, and strikes when an opening appears.

Around him, the warriors struggle on ground tangled with roots and strewn with stones. The younger soldiers have difficulty holding their positions. The veteran calls out brief orders, moves a wounded man behind the shields, and summons two companions to reinforce the threatened flank.

A few moments later, the archers stationed on the heights join the fighting. Caught between the two groups, the Orcs begin to retreat. Several vanish into the woods, pursued for a short distance before the veteran orders his men to regroup.

The fighting has lasted less time than the soldiers would have expected. Yet two men are wounded, and a third lies motionless beside the path. The veteran kneels beside him, examines his wound, and quickly understands that his companion is dead.

He remains at his side for a few moments, then rises to organise the return. The wounded must be carried, the weapons recovered, and the enemy's tracks examined. The neighbouring garrisons must also be warned, for the presence of these Orcs may herald larger movements.

That evening, when the men return to the fortification, the veteran accompanies the wounded to the room where the healers await them. He then arranges for the fallen soldier's family to be informed and writes his report by lamplight.

Tomorrow, training will resume. The young men must learn to hold their positions under fire, protect their companions more effectively, and recognise when a withdrawal becomes necessary.

The veteran knows that no exercise will ever fully reproduce what they have experienced today. Yet the experience gained, the movements practised time and again, and the trust built between the men will help them face the dangers ahead with greater confidence.

He is a Fighter, and his whole life has been devoted to this discipline.

The Profession of Arms

In Middle-earth, war has profoundly shaped the history of its peoples. Kingdoms have risen or fallen after long campaigns, borders have shifted, and entire communities have been forced to abandon their lands before advancing enemies. Defending homes, roads, and territories remains an essential responsibility, particularly where the Shadow extends its influence into neighbouring regions.

The Fighter is one of those who have made combat a demanding discipline. Training rests upon mastery of weapons, the use of protective equipment, physical endurance, and the techniques needed to face an opponent under widely differing circumstances.

This calling takes different forms according to culture. A soldier of Gondor learns to fight within an organised force, while a rider of Rohan devotes much of his training to horsemanship and the use of weapons from the saddle. A Khazâd warrior develops habits suited to the arms and armour of his people. Among the Elves, martial training belongs to ancient traditions maintained by masters whose experience may extend over several centuries.

A Fighter may serve a king, belong to a garrison, defend a community, or practise his trade under a captain who has hired him. Some become renowned champions; others spend their entire lives in more modest duties, never earning a reputation beyond the borders of their homeland.

Their skill comes above all from regular training. Handling a weapon requires years of practice, and fighting effectively beneath the weight of armour demands particular physical preparation. Exercises teach the movements, distances, and reactions needed to maintain one's balance against an opponent.

Experience completes this training. A Fighter who has taken part in several campaigns may recognise the signs of an approaching attack, quickly assess the condition of a weary troop, or understand that a narrow passage presents a danger to his companions. Such knowledge is built through marches, patrols, and encounters in battle.

The profession is thus distinguished by the depth of its martial training. It allows players to portray characters whose responsibilities, origins, and convictions may differ greatly, but who share a common mastery of combat.

The Warrior Traditions of Ancient Days

Tolkien's writings give a prominent place to warriors whose decisions shaped the history of Middle-earth. Their deeds bear witness to many martial traditions, but also to the responsibilities that accompany the bearing of arms.

In the First Age, the Noldor possess warriors of extraordinary prowess. Their wars against Morgoth give rise to many figures whose memory will long outlive the destruction of Beleriand.

Fingolfin, High King of the Noldor, remains among the most remarkable. After the ruin of several Elven kingdoms, he rides alone to the gates of Angband and challenges Morgoth to single combat. His courage and skill at arms allow him to wound his foe repeatedly, despite the Dark Lord's overwhelming superiority in power. His death becomes one of the most memorable events of the wars of the First Age.

Other traditions arise among the Men who join the Elves in Beleriand. The Houses of the Edain fight beside their allies, bringing their courage and their own ways of waging war. The tales of Húrin and Huor, of Beren, and of Túrin Turambar reveal the different forms a warrior's life may take, from service to a kingdom to struggles fought far from any army.

In the Second Age, the wars against Sauron give new importance to the military traditions of the Elves and Númenóreans. The great armies of Númenor possess an organisation, equipment, and might that the peoples of Middle-earth soon come to recognise. At the end of the Age, Elendil and Gil-galad lead the Last Alliance of Elves and Men against Sauron.

The Third Age preserves other celebrated examples. In Gondor, Boromir, son of Denethor, embodies the martial strength and courage of a captain deeply devoted to the defence of his people. His brother Faramir likewise possesses considerable military experience, but favours methods suited to reconnaissance and fighting in Ithilien.

In Rohan, the riders of Théoden and Éomer represent a tradition in which skill at arms is joined to mastery of the horse. Their intervention at the Battle of the Pelennor Fields remains one of the great events of the War of the Ring.

Among the Dwarves, Dáin Ironfoot offers another remarkable example. His long life is marked by wars against the Orcs, the Battle of Five Armies, and the defence of the kingdom of Erebor. His personal courage is matched by the responsibilities of a leader capable of guiding his people for many decades.

These figures belong to different histories. Yet they show how far the qualities of a Fighter extend beyond skill in wielding a weapon. Endurance, loyalty, judgement, and the ability to protect those entrusted to one's care give martial experience its true significance.

The Years of Training

A Fighter's training often begins in adolescence, under a master-at-arms, an experienced relative, or a community that maintains its own martial traditions.

In kingdoms with a developed military organisation, young recruits receive progressive instruction. They first learn to maintain their equipment, perform basic movements, and move beneath the weight of protective gear. Repeated exercises develop the strength, endurance, and coordination necessary for combat.

The handling of weapons requires particular attention. A young soldier discovers the characteristics of blades, polearms, and missile weapons. He learns the distances at which each may be employed and the movements needed to keep his balance when an opponent tries to force him back.

Shield-work likewise occupies an important place. It demands constant coordination between the arm that protects and the one that wields the weapon. The apprentice gradually understands that the quality of a defence depends as much on his movements as on the strength of the equipment he carries.

Body armour requires training of its own. A coat of mail changes the distribution of weight and increases fatigue on long marches. Certain forms of armour restrict movement or make it harder to cross broken ground. The Fighter therefore practises running, rising from the ground, and fighting while wearing the protection he will actually use.

Collective training forms another important stage. An experienced warrior must know how to hold his position beside his companions, recognise commands, and adapt his movements to those of the troop. Group exercises gradually develop the trust needed to face a numerous enemy.

Training also covers the ordinary responsibilities of military life. The young Fighter takes part in watches, patrols, and long marches. He learns to maintain weapons exposed to rain, preserve his supplies, and recognise the first signs of exhaustion in himself and his companions.

The years spent under a master often leave a lasting mark. Some warriors retain the habits acquired in youth throughout their lives, while others gradually alter their way of fighting as experience reveals the limitations of their original training.

Mastery of Weapons

The Fighter may develop great skill with very different weapons. His choices depend chiefly on the traditions of his people, the training he has received, and the duties he intends to undertake.

The sword holds an important place in many cultures. It may be carried as a personal weapon, a symbol of rank, or an instrument of battle used alongside other equipment. The diversity of its forms and uses nevertheless demands distinct kinds of training, with mastery dependent on the techniques handed down.

The spear is a particularly widespread weapon. It can be used in many circumstances and naturally finds a place among organised troops. Among the riders of Rohan, its use is joined to demanding instruction in mounted combat.

Axes and hammers occupy a prominent place in the traditions of the Khazâd. Their effectiveness depends on the kind of weapon, the warrior's experience, and the circumstances in which they are used. Some techniques demand great physical strength, while others rely more upon precision and control of movement.

Bows are likewise of considerable importance. Elven archers have an ancient reputation, but many peoples of Men and Dwarves also employ ranged weapons suited to their needs. Mastery requires regular practice, particularly when shooting under the pressure of battle or in difficult conditions.

Some Fighters choose to become exceptional specialists in a single weapon. They know its strengths, limitations, and most complex techniques. Others seek a broader training that allows them to meet different situations.

This diversity is one of the profession's strengths. A soldier accustomed to fighting behind a large shield does not necessarily possess the same abilities as an archer or a horseman. All may nevertheless attain a profound mastery of their craft, provided they devote the necessary years to training.

Shield and Armour

Protective equipment holds an essential place in a Fighter's training. Its use goes far beyond merely possessing durable gear: it requires the body, movements, and habits of combat to be adapted to it.

The shield is often the warrior's first true piece of personal protection. It may be used to guard his own body, protect a companion, or support a defensive line. Its effectiveness depends on how it is held, moved, and coordinated with the primary weapon.

Within a troop, shields acquire collective importance. Soldiers accustomed to fighting together know how to bring their shields close, support a wounded man, or hold a passage under enemy pressure. Such movements require mutual trust, developed through repeated practice.

Armour imposes different demands according to its design. Light protection favours certain movements, while heavier armour offers other advantages at the cost of added weight and encumbrance. Traditions and available resources naturally influence the equipment employed.

The warriors of Gondor may wear protection suited to their armies' formations, while the riders of Rohan often favour equipment compatible with the demands of horsemanship. Khazâd warriors possess particularly renowned traditions of manufacture, in which the strength of materials and the quality of their assembly are of essential importance.

Maintaining such protection is part of daily life. Fastenings must be checked, leather pieces replaced as they wear, and metal parts protected from corrosion. Defective equipment becomes dangerous to its wearer, especially during prolonged fighting.

The experienced Fighter thus comes to regard his armour and shield as the instruments of a demanding art. Their worth depends as much on the quality of their making as on the years spent learning to use them.

Fighting Alongside Companions

Most Fighters spend a large part of their careers serving within a troop. Even warriors renowned for their personal feats have often been trained in an environment where cohesion and discipline play an important part.

Collective exercises teach each man to recognise his position and understand the movements of his companions. A warrior who advances too quickly may leave his neighbour exposed; a withdrawal undertaken without warning can endanger those who remain engaged.

Trust gradually grows from such shared experience. Soldiers come to know their companions' habits, recognise those who remain calm in difficult moments, and understand who will need support when an engagement becomes particularly trying.

This solidarity does not remove every tension. Differences of character, personal rivalries, and disputed decisions may cause conflicts within a troop. Commanders must then preserve discipline without overlooking the difficulties affecting their men.

Long periods of service nevertheless foster deep friendships. Soldiers share marches, meals, nights on watch, and dangers. Some serve together through several campaigns before parting to join different garrisons or return to their families.

When a companion dies, his loss often affects the entire troop. His absence is felt in daily routines, at the table where he once sat, and in the responsibilities he fulfilled. Funerals and the stories told in his memory allow the survivors to acknowledge the price paid in battle.

A Fighter may thus remain loyal throughout his life to a company in which he once served. Old alliances, debts incurred upon battlefields, and promises made to the dead sometimes give rise to obligations that endure long after a war has ended.

The Soldiers of Gondor

In Gondor, the Fighter's profession belongs to an ancient military tradition, inherited in part from the kingdoms founded by the Faithful of Númenor.

The kingdom's forces include men from many regions. Cities maintain their garrisons, provinces provide warriors, and great houses command troops attached to their service. Equipment and methods may differ from place to place, but all contribute to defending a land threatened for long centuries by forces from the East and South.

The soldiers of Minas Tirith know the demands of guarding a great city. They watch its gates, walls, and important places, while also taking part in military operations when circumstances require.

The garrisons established along the Anduin face different difficulties. Watching the crossings, moving troops swiftly, and fighting for control of fortified positions demand particular experience. Men serving near Osgiliath or Cair Andros know the weariness of patrols and the dangers brought by the proximity of Mordor.

In the southern fiefs, traditions may differ considerably. The men of Dol Amroth, bound to the princely house, enjoy a particular reputation for valour and discipline. Other communities provide archers, infantrymen, and warriors whose training is suited to the conditions of their lands.

Prolonged wars profoundly affect the lives of these soldiers. Some spend years away from their families, while others alternate periods of service with a return to their customary occupations. Veterans pass their experience to younger recruits, especially when fighting has diminished the ranks of the most seasoned men.

A Fighter of Gondor may thus be an ordinary soldier, a guard, an archer, a knight, or an officer. The profession represents the martial experience they share, while cultural origins and personal history determine how each serves his people.

The Riders of Rohan

Among the Rohirrim, the art of war is deeply bound to horsemanship. Horses hold an essential place in their lives, and the traditions of the Mark attach great importance to the bonds between riders, their mounts, and the lands they defend.

Training often begins at a very young age. Children grow up among horses, gradually take part in their care, and learn the uses of riding in daily life. Those destined for war then deepen their understanding of the techniques required to fight from the saddle.

The handling of spear, sword, and shield is joined to a precise knowledge of the horse's movements. A rider must keep his balance, recognise his mount's reactions, and coordinate his actions with those of his companions.

Long rides form an important part of this training. The Rohirrim learn to cover great distances, conserve their horses' strength, and organise the movement of a troop whose mobility is one of its principal advantages.

The éoreds bring together horsemen accustomed to fighting under the command of their leaders. Their cohesion depends on training and on the trust developed during campaigns. The men of the Mark understand the importance of signals, mustering, and the responsibilities assigned to each group.

Their traditions particularly celebrate personal courage, but military service also rests upon loyalty to the king and to the leaders to whom the riders have sworn allegiance. The great rides belong to a shared history whose memorable events are preserved in song.

A Fighter of Rohan may therefore be an experienced horseman, a guard of the royal household, or a warrior entrusted with defending isolated settlements. His identity depends as much upon his skill at arms as upon his relationship with his mount, his family, and the other riders of his people.

The Fighters of the Northern Dúnedain

After the ruin of Arnor, the Dúnedain of the North continue to live among scattered communities. Their history remains closely bound to the wars against Angmar and the defence of the former lands of their kingdom.

The Rangers are the most celebrated expression of this tradition, but the martial abilities of their people may also be represented by Fighters whose training places greater emphasis upon weapons and techniques of combat.

Some serve the Chieftains of the Dúnedain, accompany dangerous expeditions, or help protect their people's settlements. Others preserve techniques inherited from the old armies of Arthedain, adapted to the more limited resources available to their descendants.

Equipment varies with circumstances. Ancient suits of armour may be maintained through several generations, while weapons handed down within families retain a value that goes beyond their practical use. A Fighter may bear a blade whose history has been known for centuries, even though his family no longer possesses the lands to which it was once bound.

Military training must also account for isolation. Groups are often small, and reinforcements far away. Warriors learn to act cautiously, conserve their strength, and protect those who depend upon them.

These Fighters sometimes maintain close ties with the Rangers, but their skills remain distinct. The former devotes his development chiefly to martial disciplines; the latter combines combat with broader training in travel, vigilance, and the powers of Channeling.

This distinction makes it possible to represent several forms of service among the same people without reducing all their military experience to a single profession.

The Arms of the Khazâd

The Dwarves possess martial traditions deeply rooted in their history, their Houses, and the works they have built within the mountains.

Their weapons and armour often bear witness to remarkable craftsmanship. Khazâd smiths know the properties of metals and the methods required to produce durable equipment suited to the demands of battle.

Axes hold a particularly prominent place in depictions of their warriors, but the Dwarves also use other weapons according to the traditions of their communities. Hammers, swords, missile weapons, and various forms of protection all belong to their equipment.

The conditions of battle naturally influence their training. Defending underground halls, fortified gates, and mountain passages demands methods suited to spaces that may be confined. A Fighter accustomed to the galleries of his people possesses experience different from that of a warrior serving in the armies of Men.

Wars against the Orcs have profoundly marked the memory of the Khazâd. Struggles for control of their ancient kingdoms and the defence of settlements that remained free have given rise to traditions of courage and loyalty handed down within families.

Dáin Ironfoot, who fought before the gates of Moria before becoming king of Erebor, is one of the great figures of this history. His experience, and that of the warriors of the Iron Hills, bears witness to the discipline of a people capable of sustaining their commitments across generations.

The Fighter profession allows these warriors to be portrayed without restricting them to a single specialisation. Some favour heavy weapons and endurance; others receive training suited to guarding, protecting a leader, or undertaking expeditions that lead them far from the mountains.

Their weapons may become precious heirlooms, handed down together with the stories of the ancestors who bore them. The Khazâd Fighter then regards his equipment as part of the history of his House, whose preservation and honour are entrusted to him.

The Warriors of the Elves

Among the Elves, martial training belongs to traditions far older than the kingdoms of Men.

The wars of the First Age produced great warriors among the Noldor and Sindar. Elven masters-at-arms may possess experience gained over several centuries, and some witnessed events of which Men know only the tales.

Elven longevity allows techniques to be refined with remarkable patience. Mastery of a weapon may be perfected over long periods, accompanied by the study of movement, balance, and forms of combat handed down by ancient masters.

Training nevertheless differs according to people and region.

The Noldor preserve the memory of the great armies of Beleriand and the battles fought against Morgoth. Their traditions sometimes unite the art of arms with a profound understanding of their manufacture.

The Sindar possess other inheritances, particularly those of the woodland kingdoms of ancient days. Archers and warriors accustomed to moving among trees develop abilities suited to their surroundings.

In the Elven realms of the Third Age, defending borders and watching dangerous lands remain essential duties. The warriors of Mirkwood or Lórien have particular experience in fighting among trees, while the inhabitants of Rivendell preserve the traditions of a people whose history remains intimately bound to the wars against Sauron.

The Fighter profession can represent these warriors while giving their culture its proper place. Choices of weapons, armour, and martial habits should reflect the teachings received rather than a single model of the Elven warrior.

The Warriors of Other Peoples

Middle-earth is home to many peoples whose military traditions differ from those of the great kingdoms of the West.

The Northmen preserve customs associated with their communities, hunting, and the defence of settlements. Some serve in organised forces, while others must protect their villages against attacks by Orcs or raiders.

The Beornings possess particular experience of fighting in the valleys and wooded regions. Their warriors may be called upon to defend the roads of the Anduin, accompany travellers, or protect the settlements of their people.

In the southern regions, the Haruze and the Corsairs of Umbar develop traditions adapted to the conditions of their territories. A warrior accustomed to maritime expeditions knows the constraints of ships, harbours, and landings. Others train for the defence of cities or the service of great houses.

Among the Variags of Khand, martial traditions may place particular importance on mobility, horsemanship, and weapons peculiar to their culture. Warriors from the eastern peoples likewise possess varied methods, shaped by their lands and by the wars in which they have fought.

The Hillmen, isolated communities of Eriador, and peoples settled along the borders of wild regions maintain other traditions, sometimes founded upon family instruction and the defence of clan lands.

The Fighter profession can represent all these warriors, provided cultural restrictions and the circumstances of their training are respected.

Their diversity is a reminder that mastery of arms belongs to very different historical and social traditions. The authority of a captain of Gondor, the obligations of a rider of Rohan, and the loyalty of a clan champion are exercised in different ways, even when they possess comparable martial skills.

Leadership and Protection

Experience in battle sometimes leads the Fighter to take responsibility for other people. A veteran becomes a patrol leader, an experienced soldier is entrusted with training recruits, or a renowned warrior is charged with protecting an important person.

Leadership demands qualities different from those needed for individual mastery of weapons. A commander must understand his men's abilities, assign duties, and recognise when a swift decision becomes essential.

He must also know the limitations of those he commands. Long marches, privations, and successive battles exhaust troops. A thoughtful commander seeks to conserve their strength and maintain the discipline that will allow them to act effectively when danger comes.

Authority is built gradually. Some men obey at first because of their leader's rank; genuine trust, however, grows from the steadiness of his decisions and the way he shares the hardships of those who serve under him.

Protection is a different but equally important responsibility. A Fighter charged with defending a companion, a family, or a place learns to shape his actions around that duty. His position, use of the shield, and decisions during an engagement must then take account of those whose safety he has undertaken to preserve.

These duties give the profession a profoundly social dimension. The Fighter develops his abilities to fulfil a task that often places lives other than his own in his hands.

Wounds and the Years of War

Mastery of weapons does not spare the Fighter the consequences of battle. Injuries, privations, and weariness frequently accompany a life devoted to war.

Some wounds heal quickly, while others leave lasting effects. An old fracture may make a long march painful; an injury to the hand may change the way a weapon is held. Years spent in heavy armour or on horseback also take their toll upon the body.

The Fighter learns to recognise these difficulties in himself and his companions. Medical care, rest, and physical conditioning become as important as training, particularly when a campaign is prolonged.

Wounds of memory carry another kind of burden. A veteran may retain for years the memory of a fallen companion, an unfortunate decision, or a battle from which he was one of the few survivors. Such experiences sometimes influence his way of commanding and the risks he is now willing to take.

Some soldiers become especially cautious, aware of the cost of mistakes. Others, by contrast, seek opportunities to prove that they still possess the courage of their youth. A character's relationship with his past is thus an important part of his story.

Periods of peace are not always simpler. After several years of service, a Fighter may struggle to return to the customs of his community. Former companions remain far away, responsibilities have changed, and ordinary occupations may sometimes seem unfamiliar.

The way he rebuilds his life after war reveals another kind of courage: returning to his place among his people, passing on his experience, and finding new responsibilities when weapons have at last been laid aside.

Loyalty, Glory, and the Shadow

Warrior traditions often attach great importance to courage, honour, and loyalty. These values can sustain warriors in the most difficult circumstances, but they may also become sources of conflict when personal obligations and the demands of command are opposed.

A Fighter may have sworn an oath to a lord whose decisions he now considers questionable. A captain must choose between obeying the orders he has received and protecting those entrusted to him. A champion may be asked to defend a cause whose purposes he does not share.

The desire for renown presents another temptation. Some warriors seek deeds that will secure their place in songs and chronicles. Such ambition can inspire remarkable courage, but may also lead to dangerous decisions when a character values his reputation above the safety of his companions.

The history of Boromir illustrates the complexity of these responsibilities. His courage and devotion to Gondor are beyond question, yet his desire to protect his people makes him vulnerable to the temptation of the Ring. His final defence of Merry and Pippin nevertheless bears witness to the renewal of his loyalty.

Among other peoples, oaths and ancient quarrels may have similar consequences. Wars passed down from one generation to another sometimes nourish hatreds whose origins have long been forgotten. The Fighter inherits loyalties that belong to his culture, yet remains responsible for the way he acts upon them.

The Shadow seeks to exploit these weaknesses. Anger, thirst for vengeance, and the desire to dominate may turn a calling devoted to the defence of one's people into a pursuit of personal power.

Weapons are instruments whose worth depends upon those who bear them and the causes to which they devote them. The Fighter thus discovers that mastery of combat is a responsibility as well as a skill.

The Fighter Through the Ages

The Fighter profession has a place in every Age of Middle-earth, but the traditions it represents change profoundly with the peoples and events of history.

In the First Age, the great wars of Beleriand offer a particularly rich setting. The Fighters of the Noldor and Sindar belong to ancient traditions, while the Edain develop their own forms of combat through contact with the Elves. The battles against Morgoth give rise to heroic tales, but also bring about the destruction of many kingdoms. A Fighter may serve in an army, defend a fortress, or accompany the survivors of a community forced to flee the lands they once inhabited.

In the Second Age, the rise of Númenor encourages the development of powerful military traditions. Maritime expeditions, the establishment of settlements in Middle-earth, and wars against Sauron give Númenórean Fighters varied responsibilities. Among the Elves, the armies of Gil-galad and the warriors of Eregion maintain the ancient martial traditions. At the end of the Age, the Last Alliance brings together forces from several peoples whose methods and equipment differ greatly.

In the Third Age, the profession takes many forms. The Fighters of Gondor defend a kingdom enduring prolonged wars, while the riders of Rohan maintain their traditions of mounted combat. The Northern Dúnedain preserve skills inherited from the vanished kingdoms of Arnor. The Dwarves fight in wars against the Orcs and defend their homes, while the Elves protect the last great realms of their people. Warriors from the eastern and southern regions likewise possess traditions of their own, sometimes employed in the conflicts between the Free Peoples and the servants of Sauron.

In the Fourth Age, the fall of Sauron and the restoration of the Reunited Kingdom transform the responsibilities of Fighters. Armies must now protect lands to which peace is gradually returning, keep the roads secure, and support the rebuilding of devastated regions. Old rivalries do not necessarily vanish with the end of the War of the Ring, and warriors may still be called upon to defend borders or preserve new alliances.

Each period thus gives the profession a particular meaning. The Fighter of the First Age belongs to a world of great wars and threatened kingdoms; one of the Second Age participates in the rise of the powers of Men and Elves. In the Third Age, he often protects an inheritance weakened by centuries of conflict, while his successor in the Fourth may help establish a lasting peace.

Leaving the Garrison

The Fighter's life often appears bound to a troop, a fortified dwelling, or a lord in whose service he stands. Yet circumstances frequently lead him far from the places where he received his training.

A military assignment may send him to escort a messenger, reconnoitre a region, or accompany a caravan carrying important supplies. A leader entrusts him with protecting a traveller, while an isolated community seeks his help against a threat it cannot face alone.

Some departures have more personal motives. A Fighter searches for an old comrade who disappeared during a campaign, wishes to return a weapon to the family of a soldier killed in battle, or undertakes a journey to honour a promise made many years before.

Circumstances may also force him to leave his service. A war has destroyed the garrison where he lived; his lord has died, and his heirs have disbanded the men under his command. A disagreement over an order or a military decision may lead him to abandon a career he had long regarded as his only vocation.

Life upon the roads demands changes in his habits. A soldier accustomed to the resources of a garrison must learn to maintain his equipment on long expeditions and rely upon companions whose skills differ greatly from his own.

Within an adventuring company, the Fighter brings mastery of weapons, endurance, and experience of dangerous situations. He helps protect the group, recognises certain risks associated with combat, and may organise collective efforts when circumstances demand it.

His knowledge is also valuable beyond battle. He can inspect the condition of a weapon, recognise signs of weariness in a companion, and determine whether a particular form of protection is suitable for the journey ahead. His experience of leadership may help the group reach decisions, especially when several people must act together.

His relationships with his companions gradually transform his experience. A Ranger teaches him the demands of life in the wilderness; a Bard reveals the stories associated with the places they pass; a Lay Healer helps him understand the consequences of wounds he has long regarded as ordinary.

As adventures follow one another, the Fighter discovers other ways of fulfilling his calling. He remains a trained warrior, but his responsibilities now extend to a company whose members have their own histories, aspirations, and commitments.

Portraying a Fighter

The Fighter offers an opportunity to portray a character whose life has been shaped by training and experience in battle. His culture, social origins, and past responsibilities nevertheless determine how he understands this calling.

A young soldier of Gondor may have grown up in a family devoted to the kingdom's service for generations. A horsewoman of Rohan may possess remarkable experience of long rides and seek to prove her worth before the leaders of her people. A Khazâd Fighter has received a weapon handed down by his ancestors, while a warrior of the Northern Dúnedain preserves the memory of Arnor's ancient wars.

The character's relationships with teachers and companions form an essential part of his story. Who taught him his first movements? Did he serve under a respected captain? Did an old comrade save his life during a battle? Is there a promise he made to a man who has since died?

His character depends greatly on his experience. Some Fighters develop considerable patience through long training and the discipline of garrison life. Others become fiercely independent, especially if they have served for years far from any stable authority.

Military successes may also foster excessive confidence. A warrior celebrated for his skill may underestimate opponents whose methods he does not know. Conversely, a veteran who has suffered a disastrous defeat may become overly cautious, even when circumstances demand a bold decision.

His relationship with weapons deserves particular attention. Some characters regard their equipment as the tools of a trade; others see it as a family inheritance or a symbol of their commitment. An ancient sword may preserve the memory of a departed father, while a shield passed down by a former master recalls the years of training.

The profession suits very different campaigns. It naturally finds a place in adventures devoted to war and the defence of communities, but also in journeys, investigations into the ancient past, and undertakings in which companions must face serious physical dangers.

The Fighter may become a loyal protector, an experienced captain, a champion seeking renown, or a veteran looking for a new purpose in life. His identity is shaped by the responsibilities he accepts and the bonds he forms with those who share his dangers.

Over the course of his life, he will discover that a warrior's worth is also measured by what he succeeds in preserving. Weapons give him the means to defend his own, but his choices determine the place he will hold in their history.

Weapons and Cultural Traditions

Fighter, Barbarian, and Ranger

These three professions may belong to the same peoples and use similar weapons, but their training differs.

The Fighter favours deep mastery of martial disciplines, protective equipment, and combat techniques.

The Barbarian represents training more closely tied to the fighting and survival traditions of the communities from which the character comes, with a different balance of skills.

The Ranger combines combat with a thorough knowledge of the wilderness, travel, tracking, and the powers of Channeling belonging to that profession.

These differences should be understood as orientations in training rather than absolute social categories. A Fighter may live in an isolated community and a Barbarian may serve a powerful chieftain, while a Ranger may belong to an ancient military tradition.

Tolkien's Warrior Figures

Characters such as Fingolfin, Boromir, Théoden, Éomer, and Dáin Ironfoot provide literary examples illustrating the different martial traditions of Middle-earth.

Their deeds should not, however, be automatically translated into abilities available to player characters. Some belong to exceptional lineages, possess extraordinary weapons, or play particular roles in the history of their peoples.

The Fighter in MERP-RMU represents above all a professional training whose skills develop according to RMU rules.

Shadow and Corruption

The Fighter profession has no intrinsic association with the Shadow.

The dangers of Corruption may nevertheless arise through the character's actions, particularly when he seeks domination, commits wanton violence, or agrees to serve corrupted powers.

The Gamemaster applies the corresponding MERP-RMU rules in light of the character's decisions and circumstances, without treating the mere practice of combat as an influence of the Shadow.

The Fighter comes fully into his own when his martial abilities contribute to the protection of his companions, the responsibilities he undertakes, and the choices he must make in a Middle-earth marked by war and ancient loyalties.
